Review Text: Most of the time, while working as a customer service supervisor, we were understaffed. Team members from other departments were supposed to help out during busy periods, but rarely did, which left customers complaining about ques and service quality as there was a rush to get customers out of the store. Service staff got tired of being stuck on register and often complained or regularly called in sick and cancelled shifts at the last minute, making these shifts very difficult to replace. A number of jobs were required of service staff in addition to customer service (for example cleaning, putting stock away, filling drink fridges and confectionery stands) and due to lack of staff these jobs were often left not done. Store managers and other higher up staff would then complain to me and my direct customer service manager, without recognizing that the reason tasks were not completed was due to lack of staff, not incompetence. Customers, particularly cigarette customers and refund customers tended to be difficult. Cigarette customers were often rude and demanding, as were refund customers. If you’re a store manager at Aldi, forget about work-life balance. You’ll be the last one to get it. All those work-life balance rules? They’re mostly just for show. The pay is decent, but it can feel like you’re selling your soul to the Devil. Sure, you’ll have money, but you might end up sacrificing your physical and mental health. Burnout is right around the corner, especially with crazy goals and not enough staff. You’ll find yourself doing the work of four people. Directors and area managers have no clue what it’s really like in the stores. Honestly, they should try being a store manager for three months—I bet they wouldn’t last a month, even as a store assistant. And those yearly store manager conferences? Just a horror show. It’s like a competition to see who can be the most self-absorbed. Everyone acts like they’re on a talk show, but it really feels more like an episode of "The Office," with everyone channeling their inner Michael Scott. It’s just a bunch of kids in suits pretending to be important. They could easily turn those conferences into an email, and the money spent on them could be better used to support the stores or reward the staff—anything but boosting their own egos. Hearing “without you, we are nothing” feels empty when they’re at home dreaming up more ways to pile on the pressure for those of us who are working hard. They schedule important tasks like remerch on payroll days, which is just ridiculous. Choose easy days—Wednesdays and Thursdays—when there are no specials or payroll to worry about. The distribution center is already a mess, and things that should be simple turn into chaos. What’s really missing is a more human touch—actually caring about people. We’re not robots, but it seems like the company doesn’t really care about store workers. It’s all just a cover in the contract; they’re mainly focused on making money while those who genuinely care are struggling with their health. You’re replaceable, no matter how good you are, because the ones who really get ahead are usually the favorites. We all know how that goes, right? So if you value your health, this job might not be for you.

One challenge I’ve noticed at ALPA is that remote staff can sometimes feel a real sense of isolation or disconnect from the wider community, especially in days when in-person energy is high. It’s genuinely difficult at times for remote team members to feel the same level of belonging and real-time camaraderie as those on-site. While we do a lot to bridge that gap and offer support—and I know we’re always here to help—it’s something that still needs attention. That said, recognizing this is what pushes us to keep finding new ways to include everyone, strengthen connections, and make sure every voice feels truly heard and valued, wherever they’re working from.

ALPA operates in a fast-paced, challenging environment. Those working remote need to work with challenges of limited resources, a different cultural context, surviving away from family, and problem-solving unexpected situations.

The complexity of operating across such a wide range of sectors and regions—from remote Northern Territory communities to Far North Queensland—can sometimes make it difficult to maintain consistent service delivery, cultural sensitivity, and community engagement. Balancing commercial success with social responsibility is no small feat, and there’s always a risk that some communities might feel underserved or disconnected if communication and feedback loops aren’t strong. That said, this isn’t a criticism of ALPA’s intentions—it’s more a reflection of the natural challenges that come with scaling up while staying true to grassroots values.

Working as IT support at the Arnhem Land Progress Aboriginal Corporation presents unique challenges, shaped by its remote locations and community-focused mission. One major difficulty is maintaining reliable internet and network infrastructure across isolated areas, where outages and limited connectivity can disrupt services. Delivering and setting up hardware in these regions also takes extra time and planning. Supporting a diverse workforce, many of whom may have limited experience with technology, requires clear and patient communication, as well as culturally sensitive training. You often need to troubleshoot a wide range of issues, from printers and laptops to network systems, sometimes without immediate access to advanced tools or backup. Balancing these technical demands with ALPA’s commitment to empowering Indigenous communities means your role isn’t just about fixing problems, it’s about enabling people, services, and businesses to thrive.

One of the most significant challenges at EB Games was the high turnover rate, which was not adequately addressed by management. As more employees left, the workload was consolidated and redistributed among remaining staff without any clear plans for expansion. Opportunities for personal development and career progression were limited and often appeared reserved for those willing to take on more work with fewer resources. Additionally, the company continues to rely on outdated and questionable systems. Despite having knowledgeable staff whose role is to understand the products and hardware, management frequently disregards their expertise. Instead of leveraging this insight to improve efficiency and performance, leadership tends to stick to their own views and processes, often at the expense of both time and money. This disconnect has contributed to an environment where progress is stifled and valuable resources are underutilized.

I was thinking back about my life and it brought me to one particular memory. It was about my second week working at David jones I was 19. I’m 29 now. An old family friend came into David Jones with her boyfriend she was only about 17, I had known her since she was about 5. We were talking I was happy to see her and then her and her boyfriend went upstairs to level 2. Then I saw them again on their way out, I said bye and they left. 2 minutes later security approached me and said the pair of them had stolen something. They then implied that I had something to do with it because they saw me talking to them and said if I did NOT get them to come back I would be fired. I said that’s my family friend I was just saying hello. They told me I had to contact her and get her to come back, or they would call the police and have me explain it…so I messaged her on Facebook. I was upset because the security made me believe she stole something and threatened my job so I asked her please come back I said why did you steal they are threatening my job. 5 minutes later the girl and her boyfriend came back. WITH A RECEIPT. The boyfriend purchased a wallet. She was so upset with me. She was yelling at me for accusing them (understandable.) I was disgusted with myself that I let those absolute morons in security think they could do that to someone without clear evidence of something actually being stolen. She was so upset and i absolutely understand. It is actually against the law, what happened and the way it happened is against the law. I tried to apologise to the girl but she never spoke to me again. Ever, even after 10 years. Even her mum hates me too, and I’ve known them since she was 5. Thinking back now I am actually disgusted. The security were two Oafs. Making me message her, accusing them without clear evidence, implicating my involvement and threatening my job because you are too stupid to figure it out yourself is against the law. I just thought I’d write this so David Jones can see. I still continued to work there for a while, but it was always just instilled in me from that point on I hated the operation in its entirety. It was my second job and I needed the money and enjoyed the perks which was free products at training. That’s it.

MANAGEMENT!!!! As many other reviews have stated (and I wasn't surprised to see that it was in multiple locations) the management style of this company is so toxic. The company could be successful, with their aim to be the Australian destination for high-end fashion and to give customers a pampered experience (there are still customers who crave that) but they do have a company-wide management style issue. There are just so many managers on big paychecks in the company who don't seem that necessary. Our concession companies (brands that rent space in David Jones but don't work for us) constantly comment on this. I'm not shocked the company is struggling when the people in management seem to take their roles for some perceived idea of prestige instead of actively working to fix issues or help their team achieve. They are a reactionary company. The solution to problems is to tell off the person who works under them. Higher-up managers tell off the managers in stores, and then those store managers tell off sales staff. During in-store events, we've literally had head office management stand around chatting in our sales department while drinking champagne and blocking customers from getting to the cash register or getting off the escalators. They then wordlessly handed their empty glasses to the sales staff passing by who were helping customers. I feel like this example perfectly sums up the snooty attitude of the management.

Over recent years, WMQ has undergone a troubling transformation that prioritises corporate bureaucracy over operational effectiveness. The organisation's relentless cycle of restructuring has created severe change fatigue, while a top-heavy management approach continues to generate policies and frameworks that fail to address fundamental workplace issues. Most concerning is the growing disconnect between performance and recognition. High-performing staff are routinely overlooked, while underperformance and workplace toxicity go unchallenged. New management consistently implements sweeping changes without meaningful consultation with frontline staff, demonstrating a concerning pattern of transient leadership focused on short-term metrics rather than sustainable organisational health. Despite mounting operational challenges, management's response has been to create additional layers of bureaucracy and policy groups rather than addressing core issues. The avoidance of difficult conversations and failure to implement promised corrective actions has created a demoralising environment where genuine workplace concerns are buried under administrative processes. As someone who once strongly believed in WMQ's mission, watching its decline from an employee-centric organisation to one driven by metrics and corporate policy-making has been deeply disappointing. The widening chasm between executive decisions and operational realities threatens not only staff morale but the quality of services provided to stakeholders. These concerns are raised in hope of restoring WMQ to an organisation that values its employees and maintains operational excellence, rather than one suffocating under corporate bureaucracy.
